articles.title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
articles.full_content:
U.S. air traffic was brought to a standstill Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights that lasted more than four hours.

The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, after more than 7,000 flights were canceled and airports across the country became packed with stranded, irritated passengers.

The sudden and stunning alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA said. It offered no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a White House news conference Friday evening, blamed the outage on an outdated air traffic control system in which the routers “got overloaded with data.”

By Friday evening, Delta Air Lines, United, American said they were resuming flights.

What caused the ground stop

Duffy explained that once the routers became overloaded, it led to “instability for our radar and our communications in our centers, in our TRACONS throughout the country.”

TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center.

“The TRACONS and the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said.

That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said.

Duffy said the FAA did not lose all telecom or radar capabilities but because of the instability, the ground stop was issued as a cautionary measure.

It’ll take time for the airspace to recover from the ground stop as crews and planes are out of place and staffers may have reached on-duty shift limitations. However, Duffy said he anticipates American airspace will catch up before Thanksgiving travel rush.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack and the public was never in danger.

“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.

At the time of the ground stop, there were over 3,500 airplanes in the air, Duffy said. When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights headed for U.S. destinations were airborne, according to Flightradar24, a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information.

Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system using analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.

In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport’s went black during a 90-second outage.

Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.

Mullin said earlier Friday that President Donald Trump was briefed on the ground stop.

Mullin said though authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest that. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.

Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.

Packed airports

Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.

“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”

But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News.

With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.

At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed.

“I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed.

Shortly before the FAA issued its alert, both major airports in Chicago — O’Hare and Midway International Airport — were listed on a ground stop alert due to an “equipment outage,” NBC Chicago reported.

Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement.

“Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now, our plane is heading back to the terminal, so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.”

Medical flights, such as for organ transplants, were not stopped during the ground stop, Duffy said.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare

Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

articles.title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud
articles.full_content:
The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime:

My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one:

The venerable Coway Airmega

It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality.

This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep.

The Good Night button#

Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume.

The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of).

The Coway Airmega IconS

The existing Home Assistant integration#

Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant. The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà!

status ↓

commands ↓

Why ditch the cloud?#

The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks.

Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break:

  • Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it.
  • Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well.
  • Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it.
  • Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device.
  • Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban.

On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows).

A way in#

I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server.

Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one.

All that said, two major things have changed.

First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys.

For the next few days or weeks, anyone now has a root CA thanks to eMudhra. Time to have some fun with MiTMing unwilling devices!

So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it.

The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes.

Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud.

Our man in the middle#

Initially, I tried to set it up like this:

mitmproxy

This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution?

The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi:

mitmproxy

Next, we need to configure the Pi.

I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes.

Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions.

After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with:

scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset
table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8
	set client_interfaces { # handle 4
		type ifname
		elements = { "wlan0" }
	}

	chain prerouting { # handle 1
		type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept;
		meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6
	}

	chain input { # handle 2
		type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept;
		iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7
		iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8
		iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9
		iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11
		iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13
		iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14
		iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15
	}

	chain forward { # handle 3
		type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept;
		iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16
		oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17
		iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18
		iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19
	}
}
table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12
	chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1
		type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept;
		ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2
	}

	chain filter_forward { # handle 3
		type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept;
		ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5
		ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6
		iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7
		iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8
		oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9
	}
}

Basically, the 

masquerade
rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the 
redirect
rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of 
mitmproxy
.

Also on the Pi, 

mitmproxy
runs with its web interface, 
mitmweb
, using a command line like this:

mitmweb \
  --mode transparent --showhost \
  --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \
  --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \
  --set web_open_browser=false \
  --emudhra-old

Yes, off the shelf, 

mitmproxy
has a built-in option (
--emudhra-old
) to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic.

Snooping on the fan#

Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our 

Pi-MITM-Test
Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the 
mitmproxy
web interface:

So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made a request.

The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list.

Hypothesis: The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all.

mitmproxy
has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in 
mitmproxy
’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic.

"""Serve this lab's public RSA CA only to the authorized Coway test device."""
from pathlib import Path
from mitmproxy import ctx, http

def response(flow: http.HTTPFlow) -> None:
    if (
        flow.client_conn.peername[0] == "10.42.0.93" # device IP
        and flow.request.scheme == "http"
        and flow.request.method == "GET"
        and flow.request.pretty_host == "rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com"
        and flow.request.path.split("?", 1)[0] == "/AmazonRootCA1.pem"
        and flow.response is not None
        and flow.response.status_code == 200
    ):
        certificate = Path("/var/lib/mitmproxy-ap/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem").read_bytes()
        flow.response = http.Response.make(
            200,
            certificate,
            {
                "Content-Type": "application/x-pem-file",
                "Cache-Control": "no-store",
            },
        )
        flow.metadata["coway_test_ca_served"] = True
        ctx.log.info("Served lab RSA CA to the Coway's HTTP CA bootstrap request")

Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests:

Hypothesis confirmed

We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able.

The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run 

tcpdump
on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices.

Going back to the 

POST
in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned:

{
    "header": {
        "success": true,
        "result": "S1000",
        "message": "SUCCESS"
    },
    "payload": {
        "macAddr": "<redacted>",
        "certToken": "<redacted>",
        "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com",
        "port": 8883,
        "serial": "<redacted>",
        "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0",
        "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem",
        "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key",
        "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt",
        "svcCode": "002AIR007",
        "countryCd": "US"
    }
}

So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is.

For now, we can write another 

mitmproxy
plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. 
mitmproxy
doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream:

The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now…

and after a few minutes…

There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway.

Bluetooth setup process#

When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way.

I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before. My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it, and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode.

Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C.

This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs.

Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via 

adb
, look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs.

After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this:

  • Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic 
    FFA0
    (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address.
  • Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic 
    FFA2
    :
    "P001" + protobuf {
  command: 1,
  key: Base64(random_letters)
}
  • Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address.
  • Build the configuration payload, which looks like this:
    {
  "cmd": 2,
  "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi",
  "pwd": "example-wifi-password",
  "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF",
  "type": 1,
  "macAddr": "112233445566",
  "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem",
  "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0",
  "certToken": "example-enrollment-token",
  "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001"
}
    That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to 
    FFA2
    as well.

Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes.

The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script.

I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload (

caUrl
and 
certSvrUrl
). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration.

Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan.

Home Assistant integration#

Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan. My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly.

After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant.

And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home.

All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night.

articles.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
articles.full_content:
Terminal borders that don't cost a cell

This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.

I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.

Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough 

┌──┐
by hand to have opinions about this.

The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:

So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.

Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.

Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:

Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.

What I'd use it for

  • Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.
  • Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.
  • Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.
  • Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.
  • Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.

Up close

The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:

The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:

Charts

Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:

And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:

In motion

Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:

Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:

What box characters can't do

The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.

Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.

You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.

Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little 

│
cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.

How it works

A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.

The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters (

▖▗▘▝
and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.

The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.

Styles and joints

Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.

When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher 

priority
wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.

The wire format

Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:

ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \

The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:

ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \     bottom edge, blue: an underline
hello
ESC [ 0 m                                              SGR 0 clears the pen

There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a 

cell-border
reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.

The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.

Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.

The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 

1
in 
DCS 1 + b
). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.

Prior art

Parts of this have been done before:

  • DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.
  • SGR 51 to 65: framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.
  • The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses and X/Open curses (
    WA_TOP
    , 
    WA_LEFT
    and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves.
  • IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields.

What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.

My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.

The awkward (edge) cases

When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.

Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.

Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.

On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.

Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.

Try it

The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):

git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git
cd ghostty
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dxcframework-target=native
open zig-out/Ghostty.app

Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:

python3 scripts/cell-borders.py            # the default view
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py --styles   # line styles, joints and outside fill

Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: 

p
placement, 
c
colors, 
h
blocks, 
j
junctions, 
e
halves, 
s
styles and 
l
live. 
w
cycles the stroke width, 
b
turns borders off so you can compare, and 
q
quits. Each view also has a matching flag (
--placement
, 
--styles
and so on) if you want to start on it.

The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:

git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git
cd ratatui
cargo run -p tiling-panes

Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. 

n
and 
v
split, 
x
closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press 
b
to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or 
g
to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are.

The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:

To run it:

cargo run -p cell-border-top

It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 

1
to 
4
show and hide the boxes, 
b
and 
g
work the same as in the panes demo, and 
h
or 
?
lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the 
sysinfo
dependency.

What I'd like to hear

I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

articles.title: Ggml v1.0.0
articles.full_content:
Repository navigation

github-actionsreleased this

Overview

ggml 1.0.0 prunes the deprecated public API and the legacy 

DIAG_MASK
ops, adds configurable YaRN truncation and FP8 support, and brings broad performance work across backends: few-row quantized matmuls and MoE fusion on CUDA/Metal, a Vulkan prefill FlashAttention path, a device-side MoE scheduler on SYCL, decomposed Adreno FlashAttention in OpenCL, new WebGPU kernels, expanded Hexagon op coverage, and scheduler improvements that avoid uploading unused inputs.

API changes

  • Pruned deprecated API and removed the legacy 
    DIAG_MASK_INF
    /
    DIAG_MASK_ZERO
    ops, bumping the RPC protocol to reject incompatible peers (llama/29801, llama/31946)
  • Added 
    ggml_rope_set_truncate
    /
    ggml_rope_get_truncate
    to control YaRN correction-bound rounding (llama/30206, llama/30802)
  • Implemented the backward pass for 
    TRI
    (llama/30712)
  • Added 
    MUL_MAT
    src1 precision tests and gating for 
    ggml_prec_set_acc
    (llama/31896, llama/31851)
  • Bumped the RPC protocol to v9 with faster loading and graceful failure on unreachable endpoints or failed handshakes (llama/29413, llama/30415)

Core changes

  • Scheduler skips uploading inputs that are not read and prefetches only inputs produced by earlier splits (llama/31419, llama/32100)
  • MoE cache can compute a share of the cache misses on the CPU and copy the results back asynchronously (llama/30966)
  • Meta backend raises the compute view limit for buffers with few tensors (llama/31447)

Backend changes

CUDA

  • Added few-row MMQ for batch sizes 2-24 and MMVF for BF16 few-row matmuls (llama/31533, llama/31959)
  • Added OCP FP8 support and fused NVFP4 gate/up matmuls with GLU in MMQ (llama/28413, llama/31296)
  • Extended FlashAttention with an sm70 head-size-256 config and MMA head sizes 40/72 (llama/27997, llama/30285)
  • Improved graph handling: skip compat checks on reuse, re-instantiate on cluster-dim changes, move graph state (llama/32004, llama/31284, llama/32001)
  • MoE: skip empty MMQ stream-k tiles, linearize the MoE layout, and sanitize post-bias NaNs (llama/32067, llama/31047, llama/31005)
  • Added a debug buffer pool and halved the VMM pool reservation with reserve retries (llama/31919, llama/30542)
  • HIP: use a fixed BLAS workspace and add an MFMA lightning indexer for CDNA2 (llama/31838, llama/29050)
  • Added a d_state=64 SSM_SCAN fast path and made radix Top-K deterministic for ties (llama/31818, llama/31084)

Metal

  • Fused MoE routing and kept fusable node groups inside a single command buffer (llama/31615, llama/31688)
  • Made radix Top-K deterministic for ties, added mul_mm for 32<=K<64, and switched TRI to select (llama/31084, llama/30982, llama/30711)
  • Fixed GROUP_NORM for ne03>1 and out-of-bounds accesses in the FA output and SOLVE_TRI kernels (llama/31852, llama/31662, llama/32103)

Vulkan

  • Added an Intel FlashAttention prefill kernel (llama/29357)
  • Added batched tensor copies, a test-fusion interface, and ReBAR detection (llama/31418, llama/30769, llama/31658)
  • Enabled dequantized KV with CM2, YaRN truncation, RDNA3/4 large-tile split-K, and large coopmat matmul on newer AMD drivers (llama/31526, llama/30802, llama/30280, llama/31587)
  • Added a tiled-transpose concat shader and FWHT kernels for block widths above 512 (llama/30591, llama/29772)
  • Fixed MoltenVK out-of-bounds accesses, GROUP_NORM workgroup limits, and FA scratch sizing (llama/31890, llama/31930, llama/30487)
  • Capped scalar FlashAttention at 8 rows for large heads on Qualcomm (llama/30829)

SYCL

  • Added a device-side MoE scheduler (llama/30156)
  • Made the oneDNN FA cache thread-safe and un-gated fused SDPA for Alchemist at head_dim=64 (llama/31138, llama/31574)
  • Cached the device id and reject buffers that would exceed VRAM (llama/31126, llama/32013, llama/31285)
  • Added exact rounding for CPY to Q4_1/Q5_1/Q8_0, strided CLAMP, and f16 SWIGLU_OAI (llama/31465, llama/31784, llama/30857)
  • Fixed AOT for allocations above 4GB (llama/31873)

OpenCL

  • Added decomposed Adreno FlashAttention and improved decode performance (llama/32046, llama/31633)
  • Added q6_k tiled, q8_0, and f32/q5_k multi-column GEMV kernels and f32 MUL_MAT_ID (llama/31758, llama/30947, llama/31783)
  • Added arange, non-contiguous sigmoid, repeat for f16/i32/i16/bf16, and DSV4 HC pre/post kernels (llama/31829, llama/31687, llama/31782, llama/31623)
  • Enabled multi-column GEMV by default for Adreno X2 (llama/31694)

WebGPU

  • Added batched tensor API support and returned maxBufferSize from get_max_size (llama/31473, llama/31348)
  • Added GROUP_NORM, MEAN, COUNT_EQUAL, and PAD_REFLECT_1D kernels (llama/31490, llama/31591, llama/31578, llama/31877)
  • Supported the YaRN truncation config (llama/30802)

Hexagon

  • Added Q5_0/Q5_1 support and optimized conv_2d while adding conv_3d (llama/32094, llama/31814)
  • Fused post-norm residual add into RMS_NORM_MUL and added set_tensor_n (llama/31822, llama/31744)
  • Added automatic libhtp loading and fixed 64-bit FastRPC handle truncation (llama/31781, llama/30952)
  • Fixed the host build with clang-cl on Windows ARM64 (llama/32011)

CPU

  • Switched MUL_MAT to F32 src1 and accumulate FlashAttention V in F32 (llama/31854, llama/29810)
  • Added SpacemiT GATED_DELTA_NET RVV and Q4_1 32x256 HP kernels and enabled IME2 MXFP4 repack (llama/31897, llama/31929, llama/31776)
  • Enabled the 4x4 simd_gemm tile on ARM NEON and added bf16/q8_0 VXE to llamafile (llama/32128, llama/31866)

CANN

  • Fail early when a buffer type is unsupported (llama/31270)

ZDNN

  • Accept non-zdnn tensors, invalidate compute tensors after each op, and fix release backend lib detection (llama/31824, llama/31905)

OpenVINO

  • Supported the YaRN truncation config (llama/30802)

More info

articles.title: Here's who we talked about in the podcast to succeed Jensen.  ➡️Ian Buck (VP of Hyperscale, co-created CUDA): Took Nvidia through HPC and AI phases, knows the product and the business.  ➡️Chris Malach
articles.full_content: Here's who we talked about in the podcast to succeed Jensen. ➡️Ian Buck (VP of Hyperscale, co-created CUDA): Took Nvidia through HPC and AI phases, knows the product and the business. ➡️Chris Malachowsky (co-founder, Nvidia Fellow): Central to core technologies. Almost nobody knows him. ➡️Jeff Fisher (SVP, “the tie guy”): He is technical, presents well and has been at Nvidia about 32 years. ➡️Bryan Catanzaro (ML Lead): Very technical, charismatic, research based. Any sales or business experience? ➡️Michael Kagan (CTO, Mellanox co-founder): Knows the business. ➡️Colette Kress (CFO): Sits in all the business conversations, fronts the earnings calls. Interim CEO, but unlikely permanent choice. ➡️Tim Cook (Apple): Trump posted him as a replacement. Didn't he retire? Not the sales guy like Jensen. ➡️Lisa Su (AMD): More than qualified, but at AMD. ➡️Pat Gelsinger (Ex-Intel): Currently enjoying VC life at Playground Global. Would like a challenge, but right fit? ➡️Rene Haas (Arm): He is as strong-headed as Jensen, but does he have the showmanship? ➡️Jim Anderson (Coherent): Scaling up CEO roles for a few years, but no big company experience. ➡️Naga Chandrasekaran (Intel Foundry): Foundry knowledge, technical skill, and can make deals. ➡️Raja Koduri: Unlikely the right fit. ➡️Renée James: Doesn't like stage/PR. ➡️Lip-Bu Tan: Likely to stay at Intel ➡️Sam Altman: Too volatile ➡️Johny Shrouji: Doesn't present enough Who we didn't consider: ➡️Charlie Kawwas (Broadcom): Interesting idea, it's a very public facing role but Charlie does good presentations. Best salesman? ➡️Bill Dally (NVIDIA): Chief scientist, more pathfinding, no sales experience? ➡️Jon Ross (Groq): Worked at Google, engineer, but big company leader? Got into the groove at Groq, but got the feeling he prefers getting hands dirty ➡️Madison/Spencer Huang (NVIDIA): Keep it in the family? Both work at NVIDIA in management roles. ➡️Nikesh Arora (Palo Alto CEO): No idea but was highlighted by CNBC ➡️Thomas Kurian (Google Cloud CEO): Seems sound, has the ability to make deals in Taiwan/Korea though? ➡️Sanjay Mehotra (Micron CEO): Might be a solid choice ➡️Eric Schmidt (ex-Google CEO): Big company but no silicon experience Prediction markets have Ian Buck at 41% Colette Kress at 12% Johny Shrouji at 10% Rene Haas at 9%
